title: Sky burial
hook: in parts of Tibet the body is given to vultures: a last act of generosity, told with respect

segments.voice: Yesterday, mani stones, and your line, the stone chants. Where did you leave a good word that will last a while? Today asks for a gentle heart. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

A question as old as grief: when someone we love dies, what do we do with the body? Some bury it in the ground. Some give it to fire. Some to water. On the high plateau of Tibet, in some places, the ground is hard and stony, and wood for a fire is scarce. And over that land, wide-winged and patient, fly vultures. In parts of Tibet, families answer that question with the sky. This lesson speaks of death, gently, and with respect for the families who keep this practice. Today: sky burial.
screen: `A QUESTION AS OLD AS GRIEF.` → `EARTH, FIRE, WATER.` → `IN PARTS OF TIBET, THE SKY.`

segments.voice: First, what happens, told plainly and briefly. After a death, prayers are said and texts are read for the one who has died, often for several days. Then, at dawn, the body is carried to a high place set apart for this. A ritual specialist prepares it, monks or lamas may chant, and the body is offered to the vultures. Families may watch from a distance, or not at all. Tibetans call it jhator, a name often translated as giving to the birds. Second, why the body can be given. Tibetan teachers say that by this point the mind has left. The body is like a house its owner has moved out of. It is still treated with care, but it is no longer the person. The person, in this teaching, has gone on into the in-between. Third, the generosity. Here is the heart of it. Giving is one of the perfections a bodhisattva trains in, and Buddhist stories carry it all the way to the body. In one story Buddhists tell from the Buddha's former lives, a young man in the forest finds a tigress so starved she is about to eat her own cubs. He has nothing else to give, so he offers himself. Sky burial, Tibetans say, carries that same spirit: a body no longer needed becomes food for living beings, so even at the very end, something is given. Fourth, the respect owed. This is a family's grief and a sacred rite, not a spectacle. Telling it at all asks for care. What it offers a listener far away is a quiet question: if the body is a gift, what might we give with it while we are still using it?
screen: `PRAYERS, THEN A HIGH PLACE AT DAWN.` · `A HOUSE THE OWNER HAS LEFT.` · `THE TIGRESS AND THE GIFT OF A BODY.` · `A FAMILY'S RITE, NOT A SPECTACLE.` · then, large: `THE LAST GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and go as gently as you need to. Sit comfortably and feel your body: the weight of it in the chair, your hands, your breath moving in and out. Then, if you're willing, think of this body as something you've been given for a while. Notice what it lets you give today: a hand to help, ears to listen, a voice to say thank you. Let a little gratitude settle into it. If this is hard today, simply rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sky burial. In parts of Tibet, after prayers and with respect, the body is offered to vultures: a last act of generosity from a body the mind has left. Today's word.
Your line: the last gift. Today, use your body to give one thing on purpose: carry something for someone, hold a door, sit with someone who needs company. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: In parts of Tibet, after days of prayers and readings for the deceased, the body is taken at dawn to a set-apart site, where a ritual specialist prepares it and offers it to vultures while monks may chant; Tibetan teachers describe it as a final act of generosity.
